assistant.note: The extension's one contributed color, dearReviewer.assistantForeground, defaulting to charts.purple. The rule and cat of the Assistant's Hand, and its Findings (ADR 0031).

finding.note: Gutter icons can't take a theme color: extension/media/finding.svg, finding-start.svg and finding-bar.svg (#b180d7, dark) and finding-light.svg, finding-start-light.svg and finding-bar-light.svg (#652d90, light) carry charts.purple's defaults.

extensions.colorNote: Every color is a VS Code theme variable, so no tonal ramps exist; the theme supplies all values. previewValue is VS Code's Dark Modern default, for previews outside the editor only.

narrative.overview:
The Change's code is the page, and the code lives only in the editor. Dear Reviewer writes in the margin beside it: the timeline, the Assistant's replies and the Findings list are notes about the code, never a second copy of it (ADR 0012). A margin note is in the reader's own hand and the book's own ink. Every surface takes its color, type and controls from the active VS Code theme, and must look right in light, dark and high-contrast themes without a single theme-specific rule.

The system has almost nothing of its own on purpose. Native UI comes first: tree views, comment threads, gutter decorations, codicons, quick picks and the status bar. The three webviews, each Change's overview, the Dashboard and the Assistant panel, exist only where no native view fits, and they behave like editor panels: compact, text-led, flat, divided by hairlines, readable for a whole working day. Density is the editor's density. A Reviewer who glances from the diff to the margin should notice the content, not the change of world.

Rejected on sight: the GitHub Pull Requests extension's webviews, which are slow, custom-styled review pages that look wrong next to VSCodium, and branded AI chat panels with gradients, glows, sparkle motifs or a face for the bot. The Assistant is not a character, but it writes in a hand of its own: a rule down the margin of what it says, headed by the reading cat and its name, in the one color the extension adds (ADR 0031).
keyCharacteristics: Every color is a `--vscode-*` theme variable; the extension adds one, the Assistant's, which a theme can set.
Type is the workbench font for prose and the editor font for anything code-shaped.
Flat surfaces, 1px hairlines and sticky bars on the editor background.
Controls copy VS Code's own: 2px corners, theme button colors, no flourish.
Code appears in webviews only as plain quoted text; navigation happens in the editor.

rules.name: The Borrowed Ink Rule
rules.body: No literal color values in any surface. If a role has no `--vscode-*` variable, pick the nearest semantic one and give it a fallback inside `var()`; never write a hex value. The one exception is an image the editor draws that can't take a theme color, such as a gutter icon: give it light and dark variants in the theme color's default values.

rules.name: The Semantic Hue Rule
rules.body: Hue means state, never decoration: green for passed, red for failed or a problem, the Assistant's color for what the Assistant says, Findings included, and the warning color for a Claude login billed per token. Nothing is colored only to look nice.

rules.name: The Two Fonts Rule
rules.body: The workbench font for words, the editor font for anything a Reviewer might paste into a terminal or search for in the code. No third family, no web fonts.

rules.name: The Relative Size Rule
rules.body: Sizes are `em` multiples of the theme size, so a Reviewer's zoom and font settings carry through.

rules.name: The Hairline Rule
rules.body: Separate with a 1px `hairline` or a theme tint, never a shadow, gradient or blur. If something needs to float, it should be native VS Code UI (a quick pick, hover or notification), not a webview layer.

rules.name: The One Paragraph Rule
rules.body: The Assistant's take is at most three sentences and ends by naming where to start. The overview enforces it: anything longer waits behind Show all.

rules.name: The Breathing Room Rule
rules.body: Opening a Change shows one thing. Nothing opens beside the overview, below it or behind it until the Reviewer asks.

rules.name: The Assistant's Hand Rule
rules.body: Wherever the Assistant speaks in a webview, its words sit behind a 2px rule in the Assistant's color, headed by the reading cat in that color and "Assistant" in `foreground`, at label size and semibold. The hand has no fill, so the Reviewer's filled messages stay the main flow. Nothing else uses the rule or the color, so a Reviewer can tell the Assistant's words from the Reviewer's own, from GitHub's and from Dear Reviewer's at a glance. In the editor, the Finding's gutter bar is the same rule.

dos: **Do** take every color from a `--vscode-*` variable, with a fallback inside `var()` when the theme may not define it, like `var(--vscode-input-border, transparent)`.
**Do** reach for native UI first (tree views, comment threads, decorations, quick picks, status bar) and add a webview only when an ADR says why none fits.

**Do** put styles every webview uses in `sharedStyles` in `extension/src/markdownPanel.ts`, and the overview's page styles (header, buttons, facts line, status pills, rows) in `pageStyles` in `extension/src/timeline/panel.ts`, never a copy in each panel.
**Do** give every interactive element a visible `:focus-visible` outline in `focus`, and make links in rendered Markdown reachable with Tab and Enter.

**Do** announce status to screen readers: `role="status"` for loading and working lines, `role="alert"` for the problem banner, and a visually hidden status line for changes that are otherwise only visual, such as a reply finishing.
**Do** color placeholders with `--vscode-input-placeholderForeground`; the browser's default gray fails contrast on dark themes.
**Do** check every webview change in a light, a dark and a high-contrast theme in VSCodium.
**Do** size type in `em` from the theme size, and use the editor font for SHAs, paths and code.
donts: **Don't** show the Change's code as code in a webview: no files, diffs, hunks, line numbers or syntax highlighting (ADR 0012).
**Don't** write a literal color, except in an editor-drawn image that can't take a theme color, and then only the theme color's default values.
**Don't** use shadows, gradients, blur or glow.
**Don't** brand the Assistant beyond its Hand: no avatar, mascot, face, fill, gradient, glow or sparkle motif. Its marks are the reading cat, its name, its rule and its color, and nothing else.
**Don't** build custom-styled review pages in the manner of the GitHub Pull Requests extension's webviews.
**Don't** load web fonts or set absolute font sizes.
